question: Lack of up-to-date information in Spain on wolves (Canis lupus) and their impact of livestock
In January, the Commission opened infringement proceedings against Spain for failing to submit the six-yearly report on the conservation status of wolves by the end of 20251.

According to farmers’ organisations, the report containing this data has already been drawn up and approved, but the government is not submitting it due to a lack of scientific rigour, thereby preventing a proper analysis of the current situation. Official regional data further point to an increase in attacks on livestock.

In Asturias, the number of livestock killed has risen from 2 721 to 3 257 since 2021, and Castilla-León recorded 3 979 attacks and 5 985 animals killed in 2024. Given the significance of these figures and the two-month deadline the Spanish Government has been given to respond to the letter of formal notice: 1.
Has Spain responded to the letter? If so, how has it justified the delay in submitting data it already had in its possession?

If not, what does the Commission intend to do to ensure compliance on the part of the Spanish Government? If Spain’s non-compliance continues, what additional EU protection will our livestock farmers receive, particularly following the call for the provisional application of the agreement with Mercosur, which will decimate output in Spain’s livestock farming sector?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.5.2026) On 30 January 2026, the Commission opened an infringement procedure by sending a letter of formal notice to Spain1 for failing to comply with the reporting obligation under Article 17 of the Habitats Directive2.

The required report provides an assessment of the conservation status of the habitats and species covered by the Habitats Directive (including the Iberian wolf) based on the status and trends of species and habitats, as well as the main pressures and threats affecting them. The Commission services are assessing the reply by Spain prior to deciding on its follow-up.

The Commission recalls that, under the Common Agricultural Policy3, comprehensive support is available for livestock protection measures against predators like the wolf and that EU State aid rules allow Member States to compensate up to 100% of direct and indirect costs from wolf-related damages to livestock.

Regarding the provisional application of the agreement with Mercosur, the Commission does not share the negative assessment of the Honourable Members. The agreement includes an unprecedented set of measures aimed at protecting sensitive agri-food sectors. Imports of sensitive agricultural goods are subject to very limited tariff-rate quotas that will be gradually phased in.
